title: Systemic Sclerosis
subject: Medicine
summary: Systemic sclerosis is a chronic, multisystem autoimmune connective tissue disease. It is characterized by progressive fibrosis of skin and internal organs, vasculopathy, and immune dysregulation. This condition can significantly impact various organ systems, leading to diverse clinical presentations.

sections.p: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a complex autoimmune disease leading to excessive collagen deposition and fibrosis in the skin and internal organs, alongside microvascular damage and immune system dysfunction. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by serological markers and organ-specific investigations. The American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism (ACR/EULAR) classification criteria are commonly used.
b: Skin thickening of the fingers of both hands extending proximally to the metacarpophalangeal joints (sufficient criterion alone).
Skin thickening of the fingers (puffy fingers, sclerodactyly).
Digital tip lesions (digital ulcers, pitting scars).
Telangiectasias.
Abnormal nailfold capillaries (scleroderma pattern).
Pulmonary arterial hypertension and/or interstitial lung disease.
Raynaud's phenomenon.
Scleroderma-related autoantibodies (anti-centromere, anti-topoisomerase I [Scl-70], anti-RNA polymerase III).

sections.p: Systemic sclerosis is broadly classified into limited cutaneous SSc (lcSSc) and diffuse cutaneous SSc (dcSSc), which helps in predicting organ involvement and prognosis. The extent of skin involvement is a key differentiator, with dcSSc having more widespread and rapid progression.
b: Limited cutaneous SSc (lcSSc): Skin thickening is restricted to areas distal to the elbows and knees, often involving the face and neck. Associated with CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias) and anti-centromere antibodies. Internal organ involvement tends to be later and less severe, but pulmonary hypertension can be a si

Diffuse cutaneous SSc (dcSSc): Skin thickening involves areas proximal to the elbows and knees, and often the trunk. Associated with anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies. Rapid progression and early involvement of internal organs (lungs, kidneys, heart, GI tract) are common, leading to a poorer prognosis.

sections.p: The exact cause of systemic sclerosis is unknown, but it is believed to result from a complex interplay of genetic predisposition, environmental triggers, and immune dysregulation leading to fibroblast activation and excessive collagen production. Environmental factors are particularly relevant in low-resource settings.
b: Genetic predisposition: Specific HLA haplotypes are associated with increased risk.

Environmental factors: Exposure to silica (e.g., in mining or construction) is a well-established risk factor, particularly for developing pulmonary fibrosis and polyarthritis. Certain organic solvents and epoxy resins have also been implicated.
Immune dysregulation: Activation of T and B lymphocytes, production of autoantibodies, and release of pro-fibrotic cytokines (e.g., TGF-beta) drive the disease process.
Vascular injury: Endothelial cell damage and dysfunction lead to microvascular changes, contributing to Raynaud's phenomenon and organ ischemia.

sections.p: Systemic sclerosis presents with a wide array of symptoms due to its multisystemic nature. Early symptoms often involve the skin and vasculature, while internal organ involvement can develop insidiously.
b: Skin: Sclerodactyly (tightening of finger skin), puffy fingers, skin thickening, pruritus, telangiectasias, digital ulcers, calcinosis.
Vascular: Raynaud's phenomenon (triphasic color changes in fingers/toes in response to cold or stress), digital pitting scars, critical limb ischemia.
Gastrointestinal: Esophageal dysmotility (dysphagia, reflux), gastroparesis, malabsorption, constipation/diarrhea, pseudo-obstruction.
Pulmonary: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) leading to dyspnea on exertion, dry cough. Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causing dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, syncope.
Renal: Scleroderma renal crisis (SRC) presenting with new-onset hypertension, rapidly progressive renal failure, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia.
Cardiac: Myocardial fibrosis, pericardial effusion, arrhythmias, heart failure.
Musculoskeletal: Arthralgia, arthritis, myalgia, muscle weakness, contractures.

sections.p: Investigations aim to confirm the diagnosis, classify the subtype, assess the extent of organ involvement, and monitor disease progression. Availability of advanced tests may vary in low-resource settings, necessitating reliance on clinical signs and basic investigations.

t.b: To check for anemia (e.g., from GI bleeding or chronic disease), thrombocytopenia (e.g., in SRC), or microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes on film in SRC). — Anemia, low platelets, or presence of schistocytes can indicate complications.

t.a: Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP)
t.b: To assess for inflammation, though often normal or mildly elevated in SSc. — Significantly elevated levels might suggest an overlap syndrome or infection.
To monitor kidney function, especially important for detecting scleroderma renal crisis. — Rapidly rising creatinine and new-onset hypertension are red flags for SRC.
To check for proteinuria or hematuria, which can indicate renal involvement. — Proteinuria and microscopic hematuria can be early signs of kidney damage.
To assess for liver involvement, though less common. — Abnormal LFTs may suggest primary biliary cholangitis, an overlap condition.

t.a: Autoantibody panel (ANA, Anti-centromere, Anti-topoisomerase I [Scl-70], Anti-RNA polymerase III)
t.b: To support diagnosis and classify SSc subtype, guiding prognosis and predicting organ involvement. — Positive ANA is common. Anti-centromere is associated with lcSSc/CREST. Anti-Scl-70 and Anti-RNA polymerase III are associated with dcSSc and more severe organ involvement (ILD, SRC respectively). If unavailable, clinic

To screen for interstitial lung disease or pulmonary hypertension. — Reticular or nodular opacities suggest ILD. Cardiomegaly or prominent pulmonary arteries may suggest PAH. If CXR is abnormal, further imaging (CT chest) is indicated if available.

t.a: High-resolution Computed Tomography (HRCT) of the chest
t.b: To characterize interstitial lung disease (ILD) and assess its severity. — Ground-glass opacities, reticulation, honeycombing, or traction bronchiectasis indicate ILD. Often unavailable in low-resource settings, so clinical assessment and CXR are crucial.

To screen for pulmonary arterial hypertension, assess cardiac function, and detect pericardial effusion. — Elevated right ventricular systolic pressure suggests PAH. Reduced ejection fraction or pericardial fluid indicate cardiac involvement. If unavailable, clinical signs of right heart failure (JVP, peripheral edema)
To assess esophageal dysmotility. — Delayed transit or absent peristalsis confirms esophageal involvement. If unavailable, clinical history of dysphagia and reflux is key.

To visualize microvascular damage, helping differentiate primary from secondary Raynaud's and supporting SSc diagnosis. — Dilated capillaries, hemorrhages, avascular areas (scleroderma pattern) are characteristic. Often unavailable, so clinical examination of nailfolds is important.

sections.p: Systemic sclerosis can lead to life-threatening complications that require urgent recognition and management. These often involve vital organs and can progress rapidly.
b: Scleroderma Renal Crisis (SRC): New-onset severe hypertension, rapidly rising creatinine, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia. Requires urgent treatment with ACE inhibitors.
Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH): Progressive dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, syncope. Can lead to right heart failure and death.
Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD): Worsening dyspnea, persistent cough, hypoxemia. Can lead to respiratory failure.
Cardiac involvement: Arrhythmias, heart failure, pericardial effusion. Can cause sudden cardiac death.
Digital ulcers: Can lead to infection, gangrene, and autoamputation if not managed promptly.
Severe gastrointestinal involvement: Malnutrition, pseudo-obstruction, severe reflux esophagitis with stricture formation.

sections.p: Management of systemic sclerosis is largely supportive and organ-specific, as there is no cure. The goal is to slow disease progression, manage symptoms, and prevent complications. Treatment strategies must be tailored to the patient's specific manifestations and available resources.
b: General measures: Regular exercise, smoking cessation (crucial for vascular health), skin care (moisturizers, emollients), protection from cold for Raynaud's.

Raynaud's phenomenon: Calcium channel blockers (e.g., nifedipine, amlodipine) are first-line to reduce vasospasm. Avoid beta-blockers due to vasoconstrictive effects. If severe, consider phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (e.g., sildenafil) or prostaglandins (e.g., iloprost) if available.

Skin fibrosis: Methotrexate or mycophenolate mofetil may be used for diffuse cutaneous SSc to slow skin progression. Corticosteroids are generally avoided due to risk of SRC, unless for specific indications like myositis or severe inflammation.
Gastrointestinal involvement: Proton pump inhibitors (e.g., omeprazole) for reflux. Prokinetics (e.g., metoclopramide) for gastroparesis. Small frequent meals, elevation of head of bed.

Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD): Immunosuppressants like mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide are used to slow progression. Nintedanib (tyrosine kinase inhibitor) is also approved for SSc-ILD, if available. Oxygen therapy for hypoxemia.

Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH): Specific therapies include endothelin receptor antagonists (e.g., bosentan), phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (e.g., sildenafil), and prostacyclin analogues (e.g., epoprostenol, iloprost). These are often expensive and may not be readily available.
Scleroderma Renal Crisis (SRC): Urgent and aggressive treatment with ACE inhibitors (e.g., captopril) is critical to preserve renal function and control hypertension. Dialysis may be required.
Digital ulcers: Vasodilators (e.g., calcium channel blockers, sildenafil), local wound care, antibiotics for infection. Surgical debridement or amputation in severe cases.

sections.p: Regular follow-up is essential to monitor disease activity, detect new organ involvement, and manage complications. Prevention focuses on avoiding known triggers and early intervention.
b: Annual screening for organ involvement: Echocardiogram for PAH, pulmonary function tests and HRCT for ILD, renal function tests and urinalysis for SRC.
Patient education: Emphasize cold protection, skin care, smoking cessation, and adherence to medication.
Avoidance of triggers: Minimize exposure to silica and other environmental toxins.
Early detection: Prompt investigation of new symptoms, especially dyspnea, new hypertension, or rapidly worsening skin changes.
Vaccinations: Annual influenza and pneumococcal vaccines are important due to immunosuppression and increased risk of respiratory infections.

sections.p: Systemic sclerosis can be confused with other connective tissue diseases or conditions presenting with similar symptoms, particularly Raynaud's phenomenon or skin changes.
b: Primary Raynaud's phenomenon: No underlying disease, typically milder, no digital ulcers or abnormal nailfold capillaries. Differentiated by absence of other SSc features and normal autoantibodies.

Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE): Can have Raynaud's and skin changes, but typically presents with malar rash, photosensitivity, arthritis, serositis, and specific autoantibodies (anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm).

Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA): Primarily affects joints, causing inflammatory arthritis. While RA can have secondary Raynaud's, the skin thickening and specific organ fibrosis of SSc are absent. Anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor are characteristic.
Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD): Features of SSc, SLE, and myositis. Characterized by high titers of anti-U1-RNP antibodies.
Eosinophilic fasciitis: Rapid onset of skin thickening, often after strenuous exercise, but typically spares the fingers and toes. Eosinophilia is common.
Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis: Occurs in patients with renal impairment exposed to gadolinium-based contrast agents. Presents with skin thickening but lacks other SSc features and autoantibodies.

sections.p: Certain clinical findings or laboratory results in systemic sclerosis can be misleading, requiring careful interpretation in the context of the overall clinical picture.
b: Normal ESR/CRP: Inflammation markers can be normal even in active SSc, especially in fibrotic stages, so a normal result does not rule out disease activity.
Negative ANA: While most SSc patients are ANA positive, a small percentage can be ANA negative, particularly those with anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies. Clinical suspicion remains paramount.
Mildly abnormal pulmonary function tests: Early ILD or PAH may show only subtle changes, requiring more sensitive tests like HRCT or echocardiogram for definitive diagnosis.

Hypertension in SRC: While severe hypertension is characteristic, some patients with SRC can be normotensive, especially if they have pre-existing hypotension or are on vasodilators. A rapid decline in renal function is still a red flag.

Absence of specific autoantibodies: While specific antibodies are helpful, their absence does not exclude SSc if clinical criteria are met. Some patients may be seronegative for common SSc antibodies.

sections.p: Patients with systemic sclerosis should be educated on warning signs that necessitate urgent medical attention to prevent severe complications.
b: New-onset severe headache, blurred vision, or sudden worsening of blood pressure.
Rapidly worsening shortness of breath or chest pain.
Sudden swelling of the face, hands, or feet.
New or worsening digital ulcers, especially with signs of infection (redness, pus, fever).
Sudden onset of severe abdominal pain or distension.
Any new or unexplained weakness or numbness.

faq.q: What is the difference between limited and diffuse systemic sclerosis?
faq.a: Limited SSc involves skin thickening distal to elbows/knees, often with CREST features, and typically has a slower progression. Diffuse SSc involves skin proximal to elbows/knees and the trunk, with more rapid progression and earlier internal organ involvement.

faq.q: Why is Raynaud's phenomenon so common in systemic sclerosis?
faq.a: Raynaud's is common due to the underlying microvascular damage and dysfunction characteristic of SSc, leading to exaggerated vasoconstriction in response to cold or stress.

faq.q: What is the most dangerous complication of systemic sclerosis?
faq.a: Scleroderma renal crisis (SRC) and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) are among the most dangerous complications, as they can rapidly lead to organ failure and are associated with high mortality if not promptly treated.
